How many fathers are there in the U.S.? (2026)

  • 10/11/2026
By Paul Zalewski, dad of two girls, pillow fort expert, lego enthusiast, and purveyor of fine situational dad jokes.
Cite this Research
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 8:08
Instaread

2026 update: this page uses the latest data available, the Census Bureau’s 2024 fatherhood data (published August 2026). The most recent Census headcount of fathers is from 2014.

Key finding

According to the U.S. Census Bureau, 57.0% of U.S. men age 15 and over are fathers when stepchildren and adopted children are included, and 54% have biological children (2024 data, Men’s Fertility and Fatherhood: 2024, published August 2026). The Census Bureau’s most recent published headcount is from 2014: 72.2 million biological fathers and 74.7 million fathers in all; 34.3 million men had a biological child under 18. In 2025 there were 2.57 million single-father families (father-only families with their own children under 18), a count of families, not individual men.

Updated October 2026 with the Census Bureau’s new 2024 fatherhood data. We also fixed a stay-at-home dad figure that didn’t match its source and removed two unsourced claims.

There’s no single official count of “fathers” for the current year. The Census Bureau measures fatherhood through the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP), which asks men about every child they’ve had. Its newest release, the Men’s Fertility and Fatherhood: 2024 fact sheet, reports percentages but not a headcount. The last Census report with headcounts is Men’s Fertility and Fatherhood: 2014 (P70-162, published 2019). This page uses both and labels which year each number comes from.

Data breakdown: U.S. fathers by the numbers

The answer depends on the definition (biological fathers only, or step and adoptive fathers too) and on whether you mean all fathers or fathers raising kids right now. The table shows the most recent Census figure for each.

Percentages from 2024 and headcounts from 2014 come from the same survey program (SIPP) but different years, so don’t multiply or combine them. Family counts from the Current Population Survey count families, not individual men. Census notes that its 2025 CPS figures use new (Vintage 2025) population estimates, so 2024-to-2025 changes partly reflect that method update.

What changed between 2014 and 2024

In the 2014 survey, 61.6% of men 15 and over were fathers counting step and adoptive children, and 59.5% had biological children (P70-162, Table 1). In 2024 the figures were 57.0% and 54% (P70FS-215). The Census Bureau’s 2024 fact sheet doesn’t test or comment on that change, so treat it as a comparison of two published estimates, not an official trend.

What held steady is how many fathers live with their kids. About four in five fathers of minor biological children live with at least some of them: 79.8% in 2014 and 79.3% in 2024. In 2024, 72.9% lived with all of their minor children, 6.4% with some, and 20.7% with none.

When men become fathers

Half of U.S. fathers had their first child by age 28, according to the 2024 data. Non-Hispanic White fathers become fathers later (median age at first birth 28.1) than Black fathers (26.1) and Hispanic or Latino fathers (25.8); Census found no statistical difference between the Black and Hispanic figures (Census P70FS-215). For birth-certificate data on fathers’ average age, see our page on the average age of first-time fathers.

Fathers raising kids: single and stay-at-home dads

In 2025 there were 2.57 million father-only families with their own children under 18 (a count of families, not men), about a quarter of all one-parent families with kids (Census table FM-1). The last Census count of individual men, from 2014, found 1.8 million men who were single fathers: living with a child under 18, with no spouse or partner (P70-162). Our single father statistics page breaks this down further.

Stay-at-home dad counts depend heavily on the definition. The Census Bureau’s narrow definition (married fathers with children under 15 who were out of the labor force all year to care for home and family while their wife worked) counted 231,000 in 2023. Pew Research Center‘s broader definition (any father ages 18 to 69 living with his kids who didn’t work for pay in the past year, for any reason) found 7% of those fathers were home in 2021. Details are on our stay-at-home dads page.

FAQ: How many fathers are there in the U.S.?

How many fathers are there in the United States?

The latest Census Bureau headcount is from 2014: 72.2 million biological fathers, and 74.7 million fathers when stepfathers and adoptive fathers are included. Newer Census data (2024) reports shares rather than a headcount: 57.0% of men age 15 and over are fathers, and 54% have biological children.

What percentage of American men are fathers?

57.0% of U.S. men age 15 and over are fathers when step and adopted children are included, and 54% have biological children, according to the Census Bureau’s Men’s Fertility and Fatherhood: 2024 fact sheet (2024 SIPP data).

How many fathers have a child under 18?

The latest Census headcount, from 2014, is 34.3 million men with a biological child under 18. In 2024, 79.3% of fathers of minor biological children lived with all or some of them.

How many single fathers are there?

There were 2.57 million single-father families (father-only families with their own children under 18) in 2025, according to the Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey (table FM-1). That counts families, not individual men. The latest Census count of men, from 2014, was 1.8 million single fathers (living with a child under 18, with no spouse or partner). See our single father statistics page for more detail.

How many stay-at-home dads are there?

It depends on the definition. The Census Bureau’s narrow definition counted 231,000 stay-at-home dads in 2023. Using a broader definition, Pew Research Center found that 7% of fathers ages 18 to 69 living with children under 18 were not working for pay in 2021. See our stay-at-home dads page for details.

At what age do most men become fathers?

Half of U.S. fathers had their first child by age 28, according to the Census Bureau’s 2024 data. The median age at first birth is 28.1 for non-Hispanic White fathers, compared with 26.1 for Black fathers and 25.8 for Hispanic or Latino fathers (Census found no statistical difference between those last two).

Sources

  • U.S. Census Bureau. Men’s Fertility and Fatherhood: 2024. SIPP Snapshot P70FS-215, August 2026 (2024 SIPP). Shares of men who are fathers, coresidence, age at first birth, multiple-partner fertility, grandchildren.
  • U.S. Census Bureau. Men’s Fertility and Fatherhood: 2014. Report P70-162, published June 2019. Headcounts of fathers, biological fathers, fathers of minor children and grandfathers (Table 1).
  • U.S. Census Bureau. Historical Families Tables, table FM-1. Current Population Survey, 2025. Father-only and married-couple families with own children under 18.
  • U.S. Census Bureau. Stay-at-Home Parents, table SHP-1. Current Population Survey, 1994–2023. Census count of stay-at-home fathers (narrow definition).
  • Pew Research Center. Almost 1 in 5 stay-at-home parents in the U.S. are dads. August 2023 (2021 data). Share of fathers who are home (broad definition).
